title: New Jersey bans grocery stores from using shoppers' personal data to set prices
excerpt: New law prohibits surveillance pricing, pauses electronic shelf labels for a year, and allows consumers to sue businesses that violate the ban.
content_html:
New law prohibits surveillance pricing, pauses electronic shelf labels for a year, and allows consumers to sue businesses that violate the ban.

New Jersey shoppers will have new protections starting next summer against grocery stores using their personal data to charge them different prices. Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed legislation Thursday making New Jersey one of the first states in the nation to ban the controversial practice known as surveillance pricing.

The law, called the Fair Price Protection Act, prohibits grocery stores from using shoppers’ digital history, biometric information, or genetic data to tailor prices based on what algorithms predict each customer is willing to pay. Unlike traditional sales or loyalty discounts, surveillance pricing uses your personal data to estimate the highest price you’re willing to pay, rather than offering everyone the same price.

“Surveillance pricing weaponizes your data against you,” Sherrill said during a bill signing at Our Community Grocery Store in Newark. “Companies figure out where you live, where you shop, and even what you’re Googling, and they use that data to calculate specific, often higher, prices for items you need without your knowledge.”

Don’t miss the NJ stories that matter. Sign up for our free newsletter  →

The law, which takes effect Aug. 1, 2027, allows the state attorney general or consumers to sue businesses that use surveillance pricing. Grocery stores found liable could be required to issue refunds, lose permits, and face fines of up to $10,000 for a first offense and $20,000 for subsequent violations under New Jersey’s Consumer Fraud Act.

The law does not ban dynamic pricing, in which prices change based on demand. Ride-hailing companies such as Uber and Lyft use algorithms to raise prices during periods of high demand. But the legislation does impose a one-year pause on electronic shelf labels — digital displays that can change prices instantly — while the state studies whether the technology could enable unfair pricing practices.

Sherrill said the one-year pause will give the state time to evaluate the electronic labels “to make sure they aren’t hurting New Jersey’s shoppers or workers.”

The legislation passed both houses of the Legislature on June 30.

Supporters say the law will help protect consumers as grocery prices remain elevated after the sharp increases that began during the COVID-19 pandemic. Prices in the Newark, Jersey City, and New York City metropolitan area, tracked by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, rose steeply during the pandemic and have continued to increase at a slower pace since then.

Sherrill criticized President Donald Trump’s tariffs and the conflict with Iran for contributing to higher grocery prices.

“The White House has made products in every aisle more expensive. The average family paid $310 more at the grocery store last year because of Trump’s illegal tariffs,” said Sherrill. “The sky-high prices are putting immense pressure on people across our state. Seniors are choosing between paying for groceries and paying for prescriptions.”

Opponents argued the legislation could interfere with grocery stores’ ability to offer loyalty programs and discounts. But the law explicitly states that it does not apply to discounts, promotions, or customer loyalty programs.

New Jersey Business & Industry Association President and CEO Michele Siekerka said the legislation presents a false choice between protecting consumers and improving operational efficiency for grocery stores, arguing lawmakers could have achieved both. She said policymakers made businesses “the bad guy” even though most are simply trying to communicate prices more efficiently.

“In the end, this law will compromise the very cost-saving programs that consumers rely on, particularly during an affordability crisis,” Siekerka said. “The unintended consequences could very well be the elimination of some loyalty programs, coupons, and other customer-specific discounts due to new limits on consumer data.”

But Antoinette Miles, the director of the New Jersey Working Families Party, welcomed the new law, saying AI-powered algorithms and the expansive tracking of private data for surveillance pricing have become increasingly common, allowing corporations to charge more to customers with fewer options, and without shoppers knowing they’re being singled out.

“Big corporations have turned grocery shopping into a surveillance operation, and we’re all paying more because of it. They track what we buy, where we live, and where we shop to figure out how they can charge each of us as much as possible,” Miles said. “Surveillance pricing is why corporations keep making record-breaking profits while working families feel broke. This law puts a stop to that. New Jersey is setting a model for other states to follow, and Governor Sherrill, Assemblyman Chigozie Onyema, and our legislative champions deserve credit for that.”

New Jersey is the third state to ban grocery surveillance pricing, following Maryland and Connecticut. Similar legislation has passed the New York Legislature and awaits the signature of Gov. Kathy Hochul. California lawmakers are considering a comparable bill, while Colorado Gov. Jared Polis vetoed similar legislation in June.

The bill signing came just days after Sherrill signed the FAIR Act, which prohibits landlords from using algorithmic software that recommends rents based on competing landlords’ private data.

content_html_zh:
新法律禁止监督定价，暂停电子货架标签一年，并允许消费者起诉违反禁令的企业。

从明年夏天开始，新泽西州的购物者将获得新的保护，防止杂货店利用他们的个人数据向他们收取不同的价格。 政府。 米基·谢里尔 (Mikie Sherrill) 周四签署了一项立法，使新泽西州成为美国首批禁止有争议的监管定价做法的州之一。

这项名为《公平价格保护法》的法律禁止杂货店使用购物者的数字历史、生物识别信息或遗传数据，根据算法预测每个顾客愿意支付的价格来调整价格。 与传统的销售或忠诚度折扣不同，监控定价使用您的个人数据来估计您愿意支付的最高价格，而不是为每个人提供相同的价格。

谢里尔在纽瓦克我们的社区杂货店签署法案时表示：“监控定价将你的数据作为攻击你的武器。” “公司会知道你住在哪里、在哪里购物，甚至你在谷歌上搜索什么，然后他们使用这些数据在你不知情的情况下计算出你需要的商品的具体价格，而且价格往往更高。”

该法律于 2027 年 8 月 1 日生效，允许州总检察长或消费者起诉使用监督定价的企业。 根据新泽西州《消费者欺诈法》，被发现负有责任的杂货店可能会被要求退款、吊销许可证，首次违规将面临最高 10,000 美元的罚款，后续违规将面临最高 20,000 美元的罚款。

该法律并不禁止动态定价，即价格根据需求而变化。 Uber 和 Lyft 等乘车公司使用算法在需求旺盛时期提高价格。 但该立法确实对电子货架标签（可以立即改变价格的数字显示器）实施了一年的暂停，同时该州正在研究该技术是否会导致不公平的定价行为。

谢里尔表示，一年的暂停将使该州有时间评估电子标签，“以确保它们不会伤害新泽西州的购物者或工人。”

该法案于 6 月 30 日在立法机关参众两院获得通过。

支持者表示，该法律将有助于保护消费者，因为杂货价格在 COVID-19 大流行期间开始大幅上涨后仍然居高不下。 美国劳工统计局追踪的纽瓦克、泽西市和纽约大都会区的房价在疫情期间急剧上涨，此后继续以较慢的速度上涨。

谢里尔批评唐纳德·特朗普总统的关税和与伊朗的冲突导致杂货价格上涨。

“白宫让各个渠道的产品变得更加昂贵。 去年，由于特朗普的非法关税，普通家庭在杂货店多付了 310 美元。”Sherrill 说。 “天价的价格给我们州的人们带来了巨大的压力。 老年人正在支付杂货费和支付处方费之间做出选择。”

反对者认为，该立法可能会干扰杂货店提供忠诚度计划和折扣的能力。 但该法律明确规定，它不适用于折扣、促销或客户忠诚度计划。

新泽西州商业与工业协会主席兼首席执行官米歇尔·西克尔卡 (Michele Siekerka) 表示，该立法在保护消费者和提高杂货店运营效率之间做出了错误的选择，并认为立法者本可以实现这两者。 她表示，政策制定者让企业成为“坏人”，尽管大多数企业只是想更有效地沟通价格。

“最终，这项法律将损害消费者所依赖的成本节约计划，特别是在负担能力危机期间，”西克尔卡说。 “由于对消费者数据的新限制，意想不到的后果很可能是取消一些忠诚度计划、优惠券和其他特定于客户的折扣。”

但新泽西州工薪家庭党主席安托瓦内特·迈尔斯(Antoinette Miles)对这项新法律表示欢迎，她表示，人工智能驱动的算法和对私人数据进行广泛跟踪以进行监控定价已经变得越来越普遍，这使得企业可以向选择较少的顾客收取更高的费用，而且购物者不会知道自己被单独挑选出来。

“大公司已经把杂货店购物变成了一种监视行动，我们都因此付出了更多的代价。 他们跟踪我们买了什么、住在哪里、在哪里购物，以弄清楚如何向我们每个人收取尽可能多的费用，”迈尔斯说。 “监管定价是企业不断赚取破纪录利润而工薪家庭却感到破产的原因。 这项法律制止了这种情况。 新泽西州正在为其他州树立榜样，谢里尔州长、众议员奇戈齐·奥耶玛和我们的立法倡导者为此值得赞扬。”

新泽西州是继马里兰州和康涅狄格州之后第三个禁止杂货监控定价的州。 类似的立法已在纽约州立法机关获得通过，等待州长签署。 凯西·霍赫尔。 加州立法者正在考虑一项类似的法案，而科罗拉多州州长则正在考虑一项类似的法案。 贾里德·波利斯 (Jared Polis) 在六月否决了类似的立法。

柯蒂斯·布罗德纳

柯蒂斯·布罗德纳 (Curtis Brodner) 是美国报告团成员，负责《泽西辩护者》的住房和负担能力问题。 他报告了影响新泽西州居民生活水平的政策、人员和机构，重点关注问责制和解决方案。 在加入《泽西辩护者》之前，在加入《泽西辩护者》之前，他是哥伦比亚新​​闻调查部的刑事司法报道研究员，为《纽约焦点》制作调查报道。 柯蒂斯在哥伦比亚新​​闻学院获得硕士学位，并在该学院担任托尼·斯塔比尔新闻调查中心研究员，并在纽约州立大学帕切斯分校获得新闻学学士学位。
